summary: The latest in a series of revisions of the Network Working Group's documentation conventions, updating RFC 10, RFC 16, RFC 24 and RFC 27. It restates how notes are written and shared in the series.

plainLanguage.summary: This note sets informal conventions for Network Working Group documents. It encourages people to share timely ideas, even when they are brief or unfinished.

subtitle: Early conventions for writing and distributing Network Working Group notes.

tldr.problem: People could mistake written network notes for authoritative documents or hesitate to share unpolished ideas.
tldr.mechanism: The note allows timely, informal contributions from anyone and specifies basic identifying information and a distribution list.
tldr.outcome: A note may be as short as one sentence and need not be polished or authoritative.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 30's status as Unknown and lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it. It documents early Network Working Group note conventions from February 1970.

sections.title: Who Can Write an NWG Note
sections.content:
The Network Working Group consists of interested people from existing or potential ARPA network sites, and membership is not closed. The group discusses HOST software, ways to use the network and early experience with it.

Anyone at any site may produce a note and include it in the series. This RFC is a revision of NWG/RFC 10, 16, 24 and 27.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone interested in the ARPA network can write a note. The notes share ideas about host software and network use.

sections.title: Content Can Be Informal
sections.content:
A note may contain any thought or suggestion related to HOST software or another aspect of the network. The authors encourage notes to be timely rather than polished. A note may present an idea without examples, a specific suggestion without background, or a question without an attempted answer. One sentence is the minimum length.

The RFC says these permissive conventions are meant to counter the assumption that written statements are authoritative and to reduce hesitation about publishing unpolished work.
sections.plainLanguage: A note can be a short question, suggestion or unfinished idea. It does not have to be polished or authoritative.

sections.title: Form and Distribution
sections.content:
Each note should include the heading Network Working Group and a Request for Comments: X entry with a serial number, the author's name and affiliation, a date, and a title. Steve Crocker at UCLA assigns serial numbers, and titles do not have to be unique.

One copy is sent from the author's site to each person on the listed distribution list. Local reproduction may be used if more copies are wanted. The document also lists current addresses for the recipients and asks readers to correct them when needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each note needs an identifying number, author, date and title. A copy goes to each named recipient, and people can make local copies.
